title: Game 9: Magnus vs Hans
notes: Game 9 of 12 in the experiment, from the Caro-Kann Defence. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

My e4 knight is unsupported and attacked by the bishop, so I reposition it with tempo: 5.Ng3 hits Bf5 and forces it to g6, after which h4-h5 gains space (the standard Caro-Kann main line). I checked Black's only check, 5...Qa5+, which is harmlessly met by 6.Bd2 or 6.c3 gaining a tempo — nothing of mine is loose.

My bishop on f5 is attacked by the knight on g3, and retreats like Bxc2 (Qxc2) or Bd3 (Bxd3) just lose a piece, while Bg6 keeps the bishop on its ideal diagonal, defended and safe from h4-h5 ideas for now. This is the standard Caro-Kann Classical setup, after which I'll follow with Nf6, e6, Bd6/Be7 and castle.

This is the Caro-Kann Classical where the standard plan is 6.h4, immediately questioning the g6 bishop and threatening h5 to win space or the bishop, while my king will later go to the queenside or castle short only after the h-pawn has done its job. Black has no checks or captures here (Qb6 hits d4/b2 but is met by Nf3/c3), so the pawn thrust is safe and gains a tempo rather than weakening a castled position.

This is the Classical Caro-Kann main line; after 6.h4 I must stop h5 from trapping my bishop, and 6...h6 is the standard move giving the bishop a retreat square on h7 after 7.h5. Alternatives like 6...h5 leave a permanent weakness and 6...Bxc2 simply loses the bishop to Qxc2.

This is the main-line Caro-Kann and the book move 7.Nf3 develops a piece toward the strong e5 square while keeping everything defended; the greedy 7.Bxh6 just loses a piece to gxh6. I checked Black's only check, 7...Qa5+, which hits nothing loose and is answered by 8.Bd2 or 8.c3.

This is the main-line Classical Caro-Kann; note that 7...Qxd4 just loses the queen to Nxd4 and 7...Bxc2 invites Qc1 trapping the bishop. I'll play the book move 7...Nd7, developing and preparing to meet 8.h5 Bh7 9.Bd3 with the usual exchange on d3 and e6.

This is the main-line Caro-Kann Classical, where 8.h5 is theory: it takes the g6 square away and forces the bishop to the passive h7, since 8...Bxh5 9.Nxh5 simply wins a piece. I checked Black's only check, 8...Qa5+, which I answer with c3 or Bd2 and still collect the bishop with hxg6; the tempting 8.Bxh6 just loses a piece to gxh6.

This is the main-line Caro-Kann; 8...Bxh5 just drops a piece to 9.Nxh5, and 8...Bxc2 loses to 9.Qxc2, so the bishop must retreat. Bh7 keeps the bishop on the key diagonal, awaiting Bd3 to trade off White's strong light-squared bishop before developing with e6.

This is the Caro-Kann Classical main line, where 9.Bd3 is theory: it offers the trade of my bishop for Black's light-squared bishop, and after 9...Bxd3 10.Qxd3 my queen sits actively while Black still must solve development. I checked Black's checks — no Qa5+ or Qb4+ wins anything since Bd2/c3 answer them — and no piece of mine is left loose.

This is the main-line Classical Caro-Kann, where the standard plan is to trade off my light-squared bishop that has been chased to h7, relieving my cramped position. After 9...Bxd3 10.Qxd3 I follow up with e6, Ngf6 and Qc7/Qa5, developing smoothly; alternatives like Bg6 let White keep harassing me with Ne5 or Nf5 ideas.

Recapturing with the queen is right here even though my rule usually prefers the minor piece, because cxd3 would wreck my structure and leave a doubled isolated pawn with no compensation — here only the queen or the c-pawn can take, and Qd3 is well placed on the b1-h7 diagonal. I checked Black's checks: after 10.Qxd3 the only one is ...Qa5+, which I answer with c3 or Bd2 keeping everything defended, and Bxh6 fails to gxh6.

This is the main-line Caro-Kann Classical; with the light-squared bishops traded, the book continuation is to develop the queen to c7, eyeing the open c-file and preparing e6, Ngf6 and queenside castling. I checked that White has no immediate tactic: 11.Ne5 Nxe5 12.dxe5 even loses the e-pawn to Qxe5+, and Qg6 only hits the defended f7 pawn.

This is the standard Caro-Kann classical line, and the main developing move 11.Bd2 both covers the a5-e1 diagonal (killing any ...Qa5+/...Qb4+ ideas that my rule 6 warns about) and prepares O-O-O, after which my king is safe and my rooks connected. I rejected Bf4 because ...Qa5+ gains a tempo, and Bxh6 gxh6 is just a piece for a pawn with no follow-up.
Qxg3 just loses the queen to fxg3, and Qe5+ runs into Nxe5, so I stick with the solid Caro-Kann setup. I'll play e6 to open the f8-bishop, prepare Ngf6 and castling, keeping a sound structure.

This is the standard Caro-Kann classical structure and 12.O-O-O is the natural developing move, getting my king out of the centre and connecting rooks while the d2 bishop is guarded by the king and the d1 rook backs up d4; I checked Black has no checks at all (Bb4 and Qa5 only hit the defended d2 bishop and a2, answerable by a3/Kb1/c3). Bxh6 just loses a piece to gxh6, so I castle long and keep the h5/g3 kingside space.

This is the main-line Classical Caro-Kann, and I need to develop my kingside while keeping the option of castling long; Qxg3 is a trap since f2 simply recaptures. 12...Ngf6 is the theoretical move, preparing 0-0-0 and meeting 13.Ne5 with Nxe5 or 13.Ne4 with Nxe4.

This is the main-line Caro-Kann and 13.Ne4 is the natural theory move, offering a trade where e4 is covered twice (Qd3 and Nf3) after ...Nxe4, so any capture chain favours me. Black has no checks available (Bf8 can only reach b4 as a non-check, and Bd2 is guarded by both Kc1 and Rd1), and none of my pieces sit loose after the exchange.

This is the standard Classical Caro-Kann position, where trading knights on e4 is the main line; grabbing on h5 loses a piece to Rxh5. After 14.Qxe4 nothing of mine hangs and I can follow with Be7 and castling, so I'll make the trade.

Black's knight on e4 is now undefended after the exchange on e4 — no pawn or piece covers it — so I simply recapture with the queen to restore material; my queen on e4 is attacked by nothing, and Bd2 stays guarded by Rd1 and the king. I checked 14.Bxh6 first, but 14...Nxd2 15.Rxd2 gxh6 only swaps bishop for knight and leaves me nothing, while 14...Nxf2 even forks my queen and rook.

My knight on d7 can jump to f6 hitting the white queen, gaining a tempo for development — and Qxc6+ is impossible since b7 guards it. After the queen retreats I'll follow with Bd6 and castle, reaching the comfortable standard Caro-Kann setup.

Black's 14...Nf6 hits my queen on e4, and every "defend" idea (Rde1) just loses queen for knight, while Qxe6+ (fxe6) and Qxc6+ (bxc6) walk into pawn recaptures; retreats to d5, g4, h7, f5 and g6 are all captured by the knight or a pawn. Qe2 is the safe, active square — undefended but unattackable, keeping the e-file for Rhe1 and supporting Ne5 ideas, and Black has no checks (Qa5 hits Bd2 which Rd1 and my king guard).

Nxh5 just loses a piece to Rxh5, so I should develop instead; Bd6 brings the bishop out, prepares queenside castling, and if White tries Bf4 I simply take with Bxf4+ since nothing recaptures on f4. This keeps my solid Caro-Kann structure intact with no weaknesses.

I first checked the tempting moves and found traps: Qxe6+ drops the queen to fxe6, Bf4 and Bg5/Bxh6 lose a piece (Bxf4+ is check once d2 is vacated, hxg5/gxh6 recapture), and Ba5/Bb4/Bc3 hand Black the annoying Bf4+ by opening the c1-f4 diagonal. Ne5 plants the knight on a strong central square, and if Bxe5 dxe5 the pawn is safely guarded by Qe2 (Qxe5?? just loses the queen since nothing recaptures) while kicking the f6 knight and leaving me the good bishop plus the open d-file against the uncastled king.

White's knight on e5 is his only active piece and it creates Nxf7 forking tricks if I castle, so I'll eliminate it; after 17.dxe5 my knight must move and Nd5 is ideal, blocking the d-file and sitting on a square protected by c6, leaving White with a passive bishop against my strong knight. I checked Bxh6 sacrifices for White and they fail because my rook on h8 covers h6 while his h5 pawn can't recapture.

Black's bishop took my knight on e5, so I must recapture, and I checked the counts: Qxe5 is met by Qxe5 (c7-d6-e5 diagonal) forcing dxe5 and a queen trade, whereas 17.dxe5 keeps queens, hits Nf6 with tempo, and e5 is defended by my Qe2 along the open e-file. Tactical checks: ...Ne4 or ...Ng4 simply drops the knight to Qxe4/Qxg4, ...Nxh5 loses to Rxh5, and ...Qa5 allows exf6 with a crushing g7 pawn, so after ...Nd7 I can bolster e5 with f4.

The e5 pawn is undefended and my knight on f6 was attacked, so Qxe5 solves the threat and wins a pawn; after 18.Bf4 I simply step aside with Qc5, and Bxh6 doesn't work since h6 is doubly defended by g7 and Rh8. Nxh5 loses a piece to g4 trapping the knight, so the queen capture is clearly best.

Black's queen just landed on e5 and I checked every possible defender: the f6 knight covers d5/e4/g4/h5/h7/d7/e8/g8 but not e5, and there's no d6 or f6 pawn, so e5 is completely undefended with a clear e-file from my queen on e2. Qxe5 wins the queen outright, and Black has no recapture or intervening check, so I take it instead of the losing 18.Bxh6 gxh6.

I'm already down heavy material after the queen trade went wrong, and my knight on f6 plus h6 are both hanging on the overloaded g7 pawn (Bxh6! would win the knight), so I need to move the knight. Nd7 does that while attacking the queen on e5, gaining a tempo to then consolidate with Kf8 or castling long.

My queen on e5 is attacked by Nd7, so I must move it; Qxe6+ fails to fxe6 and Qb8+ loses to Nxb8 (the d7 knight covers b8), both traps I nearly missed. Qxg7 moves the queen to safety while grabbing a genuinely undefended pawn — Rh8 doesn't cover g7, f7 can't capture there, and Nd7 reaches only b8/b6/c5/e5/f6/f8 — and if 19...Rh7 then 20.Qxh7 wins a rook, keeping my queen-for-pawn advantage with no Black checks available.

My h8 rook is hanging to the queen on g7, so I must address that immediately — Rh7 loses to Qg8+ and Rf8 just concedes h6 for free. Rg8 attacks the queen (Qxg8+ Ke7 would lose the queen for a rook), forcing her to retreat while I pick up the g2 pawn in return.

Black's Rg8 is completely undefended — the a8 rook's defence along the eighth rank is blocked by the king on e8, and the king itself doesn't touch g8 — so Qxg8+ simply wins a whole rook with check, and after the king steps aside my queen on g8 even eyes the loose a8 rook. I checked that nothing can capture on g8 and that my own king on c1 faces no checks.

Nf8 just loses the knight for nothing after Qxf8+ Kxf8, leaving me a full rook and bishop down with no compensation. Ke7 steps out of check, keeps my knight, and my rook on a8 can activate; f7 is defended by my king so Qg7/Qf7 ideas don't win more material immediately.

The a8 rook is completely undefended — the knight on d7 and the b7 pawn don't cover it — so Qxa8 wins a full rook, and after any ...Nb6 trying to trap my queen she has the whole eighth rank (b8–h8) to escape plus Qxa7. Qxf7+ only grabs a pawn by comparison.

I'm hopelessly down material, so I just want the most resilient setup: Nc5 activates the knight, covers b7 so the queen can't munch my queenside pawns for free, and keeps my king shielded. Nb6 would attack the queen but simply loses the knight to Qxa7.

Qxb7+ loses the queen because the c5 knight guards b7, and Qd8+/Qe8+/Qf8+ are all met by Kxd8 etc. since my queen is undefended there. Qxa7 is completely safe (no black piece attacks a7), wins a pawn, and from a7 my queen also attacks the loose knight on c5 along the a7-c5 diagonal.

I'm hopelessly behind on material (queen and two rooks plus a bishop against a lone knight), so I'm just looking for the most active try and any chance to trade off a piece. Nb3+ and Nd3+ simply lose the knight to a pawn capture, so I'll play Ne4, hitting the bishop on d2 and hoping to win it back.

I'm up a queen, rook and bishop, so the only real danger is the loose Ne4, which currently hits both my undefended f2 pawn (forking Rd1/Rh1) and my Bd2; Qd4 attacks the undefended knight while simultaneously guarding f2, d2, c3 and c5, so the knight must retreat to f6 or g5 with nothing achieved. I checked Black has no checks (the knight can't reach d3/b3/e2/a2 in one move) and d4 is attacked by nothing.

My knight on e4 is attacked by the queen, and I'm desperately behind on material, so I need the most active resource. Nxf2 grabs a pawn and forks both rooks on d1 and h1 — White can only save one, so I win a rook for my knight and get some play.

Black's knight on f2 is forking both my rooks on d1 and h1, but it is completely undefended — neither the f7 pawn nor the e7 king covers f2, and my queen on d4 hits it along the clear d4-e3-f2 diagonal. Qxf2 simply wins the knight for nothing, leaving queen, bishop and two rooks against bare pawns with no counter-threats.

I'm hopelessly down material (queen, bishop and both rooks against bare pawns), so my only aim is to avoid immediate checks and mate. With my king on e7, Bb4+ and Rd1-d7 ideas hit at once, so I tuck the king back to e8 behind the f7 pawn where there's no instant check.

I nearly played Qxf7+ but the black king on e8 defends f7, so Kxf7 would win my queen — exactly the "recount the defenders" trap. Instead Bb4 clears the d-file (Rd1 covers d7/d8) while the bishop covers e7 and f8, leaving the king no legal moves, and next move Qf8 is mate since Bb4 guards f8.

I'm down a queen, so I just want to make my king as safe as possible and avoid immediate mating nets. 25...c5 loses the pawn to Bxc5, while 25...f6 blocks the f6 square from the queen and opens f7 for my king, so it's the most solid practical try.

Black's f6 pawn is completely undefended (the e6 pawn guards d5/f5, not f6), so Qxf6 is free material; crucially the queen on f6 then covers d8 and e7, so I threaten Rd8#. Rd8+ right now would fail to Kxd8 since nothing guards d8 — exactly the "name the defender" check my notebook demands.

My position is lost — White threatens Rd8# since the queen on f6 covers d8, e7 and f7, and none of my pawn moves can stop it. I'll play c5 to at least hit the bishop on b4 and hope White grabs the pawn instead of mating.
Rd8 is mate: the rook lands on d8 protected by the f6 queen along the f6-e7-d8 diagonal, so Kxd8 is illegal, while e7, f7 and f8 are all covered by the queen and rook.

new_lessons: [middlegame] Play every capture chain on a square to the end, recounting attackers and defenders after each trade; a piece never defends the square it moves to Example: ...Qc3 "forked" rooks but bxc3 won the queen; 27...Rf5 was "backed" by the rook that had just moved

[middlegame] Before any quiet or developing move, list every enemy check and every capture on your loose pieces; if one wins material, pick another move Example: 11.Bc4?? Qh4+ 12.Bf2 Qxc4 with f3 played and king uncastled, 55%→8%

[middlegame] After castling on the opposite wing, spend a tempo on Kb1/Kh1 prophylaxis before starting operations, instead of releasing central tension Example: Caro-Kann: 13.Ne4 traded at once; Stockfish preferred 13.Kb1 then Rh4 with a lasting attack

[middlegame] When you have more space or an attack, avoid trades that ease the defence; instead improve your worst-placed piece and keep pieces aimed at the enemy king Example: 13.Ne4 and 15.Qe2 swapped attackers off; Kb1, Rh4 and Ne5 build-ups scored better

[middlegame] Before trading a minor piece, play the recapture: if a pawn recapture opens a file/diagonal toward your king or leaves pawns loose, keep the piece Example: 17...Nc4 18.Bxc4 dxc4 opened the e-file for Re4 and left c4 hanging, 51%→9%

[middlegame] When a wing pawn is fixed (h5 vs h6), lift the rook to the 4th/5th rank (Rh4) and swing it to the other side instead of waiting Example: Caro-Kann after 8.h5 h6: Rh4 was the engine's main idea in several positions, not more piece trades

[middlegame] Each move, name your undefended pieces and the entry squares (c2, d3, g4, your 6th/7th rank) an enemy unit can reach; guard the loosest first Example: Loose bishop plus loose pawn gave Black free tempi ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5, then a rook invaded d6-c6

[middlegame] Keep a knight or bishop on an advanced square only if a pawn can support it; retreat before enemy pawns remove every escape square Example: Unsupported Ne4 had no safe retreat after e5/d6; Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns

[middlegame] Never push pawns in front of your own castled king while an enemy bishop or queen eyes those squares; answer a wing storm with a central break Example: 17.g3 invited ...fxg3 and ...Bxh3; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[middlegame] When a bishop pins your knight against king or loose rook, kick the pinner with a3/h3 or Bd2 rather than defending passively with the queen Example: 12.Qd2 let ...Nc5-e4 pile on; 12.a3 questioned Bb4 at once, 59%→54%

[middlegame] When a rook can invade the enemy second rank hitting loose pawns, prefer that to any equal trade; with exposed kings, activity beats simplification Example: Instead of 17...Nc4, 17...Rf2 grabbing h2 and tying White down was winning

[opening] Delay the central break (d5/e5) until minors are out and the king is castled; when two units can recapture, use the minor piece, not the queen Example: 8...d5 exd5 left a backward pawn, 48%→42%; 10...Qxd5? 11.Qxd5 lost a tempo, 45%→38%

[endgame] Before trading into a pure pawn endgame, count both kings' distance to every pawn and the race in moves; equal material loses if his king is faster Example: 28...Rxe5 29.Rxe5 looked drawable 4v4, but White's central king outpaced mine, 50%→6%

[endgame] With extra material, trade one-for-one but never your last extra piece; first cut off his king and take the 7th, push a pawn only with escort Example: Refusing 31.Rd5 dropped 94%→61%; later 59...b5 pushed an unescorted pawn instead of Rd5

[endgame] Keep extra pawns connected, stay inside the square of every passer, and before each move check enemy Kx-captures and stalemate traps Example: 66...Qc3+? Kxc3 drew a won queen endgame; 29...dxc4 scattered a6/c4/c6 into losable pawns
